title: The cook's instructions
hookLine: Dogen's instructions for the cook: treat rice and water as your own eyes

lines: AN OLD COOK IN THE NOON SUN.
cards: Midday, blazing sun, stone pavement too hot to stand on. An old monk with no hat, a bamboo staff in his hand, is spreading mushrooms out to dry, sweat pouring off him.
A young visitor from Japan, Dogen, asks him: why are you doing this yourself? Why not let a helper do it? The old cook answers, in paraphrase: others are not me.
Dogen tries again: then why now, in this heat? The answer: if not now, when? Dogen tells this story in a short text he wrote for monastery cooks.

teach.h: THE KITCHEN IS A MEDITATION HALL.
teach.b: First, the kitchen is a meditation hall. In a Zen monastery the head cook, the tenzo, is a senior post, given to someone whose practice is trusted.
Dogen's instructions treat the kitchen as a meditation hall: planning meals, washing rice, tending the fire, none of it beneath anyone, none of it separate from the way. Second, the eyes.

teach.h: RICE AND WATER, LIKE YOUR EYES.
teach.b: Dogen tells the cook, in paraphrase, to look after the rice and water as carefully as your own eyes: gently, never carelessly, never roughly.
He also says to look for sand while washing the rice, and for rice while throwing out the sand, so not one grain is lost and not one stone gets through.

teach.h: NO PLAIN DISH, NO FANCY DISH.
teach.b: Third, no plain dish, no fancy dish. A simple broth made with care, he says in paraphrase, is no lower than a rich dish, and a rich dish is no higher. Every pot gets the same eyes.
Fourth, not someone else, not later. The old cook turned down the easy way out twice. Dogen writes that he had nothing more to say, and walked away seeing how much the cook's work matters.

The way was in this too: the mushrooms, the heat, done by your own hands, now. For anyone who has stood at a stove at the end of a long day, that's a striking thought: the pot of pasta is not in the way of a deeper life.

how: In Soto Zen monasteries the head cook (tenzo) is a senior role, and Dogen's Instructions for the Cook (Tenzo Kyokun) is still read as a guide to treating kitchen work, and daily work in general, as practice.

o: rules for which foods a Zen monk may and may not eat
a Zen recipe book of simple vegetarian temple meals
Dogen's teaching: cook every meal as practice, with full care

games.q: you're the old cook, drying mushrooms in the noon sun. a young visitor asks why you don't let a helper do it. what do you say?
o: I'll do it later when it's cooler.
games.why: as Dogen tells it: others are not me. and when asked why now: if not now, when? Dogen writes that he walked away seeing how much the cook's work matters.

practice: Bring to mind the next thing you'll prepare, even toast or a cup of tea, and picture your hands doing it: the water running, the bread, the knife.
Now picture doing it the tenzo's way, as carefully as you'd handle your own eyes, with no hurry and nothing beneath you. Notice what changes, then let it go and rest in the breath.

wordCard.voice: The cook's instructions. Dogen's teaching for the monastery cook: treat the rice and water as your own eyes, and cook every meal as practice. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: Tenzo Kyokun, Dogen's 'Instructions for the Cook'.
